title: The rock at Siccar Point
teaches: Unconformities, the cycle that makes and unmakes rock, and how Hutton read deep time in a single cliff

blocks.text: In June 1788 three men took a boat along the coast of Berwickshire, in southeast Scotland, looking for a place where two particular formations of rock met. They were James Hutton, a farmer, physician and chemist who had spent twenty years working out how the land was made; John Playfair, a mathematician; and Sir James Hall, the young owner of the nearby Dunglass estate who a decade later would melt basalt in a furnace (lesson 4). They found what they were looking for at a rocky headland called **Siccar Point**.

blocks.caption: The Berwickshire coast east of Dunglass. Siccar Point is the small headland where the cliffs turn south.

options.title: Siccar Point, Berwickshire
options.alt: A shaded relief map of the Berwickshire coast with the North Sea to the north, Cockburnspath inland to the west and Siccar Point on the coast to the east.

blocks.text: Two sets of rock meet at the base of the cliff there. The lower set is grey sandstone and mudstone in beds a few centimetres to a metre thick, standing almost on end like books on a shelf. Resting on their worn-down edges is a reddish sandstone whose beds lie nearly flat, tipped gently toward the sea. The boundary between the two is sharp enough to lay a hand across, and at its base the red rock is full of angular fragments broken from the grey rock below.

blocks.caption: Hutton's unconformity at Siccar Point. The grey beds stand on end in the foreground, and the red sandstone lies across their worn tops.

blocks.text: Hutton had found the same arrangement the year before, at Jedburgh in the Scottish Borders and on the Isle of Arran, though neither exposure was as clean as the wave-washed ledges at Siccar Point. His reading of that contact became one of the founding arguments of geology.

blocks.caption: Above, John Clerk of Eldin's 1787 drawing of the unconformity at Jedburgh, with flat beds resting on upright ones. Below, the same section photographed in 2003.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: At Siccar Point, grey beds standing nearly vertically are overlain by gently tilted red sandstone.
The lowest layer of the red sandstone contains angular fragments broken from the grey rock beneath it.

blocks.text: Steno's principles from lesson 1, original horizontality and superposition, are enough to reconstruct what happened at the cliff. The grey beds were laid down as sand and mud on a sea floor, so they began horizontal; some still preserve ripple marks and graded layers (coarse at the bottom and fine at the top) that only form as loose sediment settles through water. Because those beds now stand on end, they must have been tilted through roughly 80 degrees after they hardened. Brittle rock near the surface shatters under that kind of strain, so the folding had to happen kilometres underground where the crust was warm and under heavy pressure, during the same sort of collision that buried the Highland muds in lesson 5.

The tops of the upright grey beds are planed off along a single, gently uneven surface. Whatever once stood above them, including the upper arches of the folded beds, was worn away while that surface sat exposed to rain, frost and running water. Only later was the red sand spread over the bevelled edges, and the rubble of grey rock trapped in its lowest layer confirms that the grey beds were already hard, upright and eroding when the red sediment arrived.

A buried erosion surface like this, separating two rock sequences of very different ages, is an **unconformity**. It marks a gap in the record, a span of time during which rock at that spot was being removed rather than laid down. Siccar Point is the most famous example in the world, still known to geologists as Hutton's Unconformity.

blocks.caption: How the cliff at Siccar Point was made, in five stages. The red dashed line is the unconformity.
blocks.task: Advance the timeline to the modern cliff and compare how different rates of erosion and deposition change the total time elapsed

blocks.text: Every stage in that sequence can be seen operating today: rivers carry sand and mud to the sea, earthquakes lift coastlines a metre or two at a time, and weather wears down hills. The interactive diagram accounts for roughly 11 kilometres of rock laid down and stripped away in total; at a tenth of a millimetre per year, a typical long-term average, the full sequence takes more than 100 million years. Each individual step is easy enough to picture, once you accept how slowly those processes run when measured and how much time the whole succession therefore requires.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: An unconformity is a buried erosion surface between two rock sequences of different ages, recording a gap in time.
At Siccar Point, that gap spans the folding of the grey beds, their uplift into mountains, and the erosion of those mountains to a plain.
Every step in the sequence operates today at measurable, slow rates.

blocks.text: Hutton had no way to measure geological ages in years, though he knew that rivers move sediment slowly, that coastlines barely shift in a human lifetime, and that Roman roads and walls in Britain had weathered very little over sixteen centuries. If the processes that built Siccar Point ran at rates anything like those, then laying down kilometres of grey sediment, folding it, raising it into mountains, planing the mountains down, and burying their roots under red sand required a span of time far beyond ordinary historical reckoning.

blocks.caption: James Hutton, in a portrait by Henry Raeburn.

blocks.text: Many educated Europeans of the late eighteenth century took the Earth to be about 6,000 years old, an estimate calculated in the seventeenth century from biblical genealogies, most notably by Archbishop James Ussher, who placed creation at 4004 BC. Some naturalists had already pushed past that figure: in 1778 the Comte de Buffon timed how long heated iron spheres took to cool and estimated an age of roughly 75,000 years for the Earth. Hutton went much further, writing at the end of his 1788 paper that in the geological record "we find no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end." The rocks preserved cycle after cycle of the same processes, and the earliest rocks he could find were themselves built from the debris of still older land.

Recalling the boat trip to Siccar Point years later, Playfair wrote that "the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time." His clear, fluent *Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory of the Earth* (1802) did far more than Hutton's own dense prose to win readers over. Explaining the geological past through processes still observable in the present became known as **uniformitarianism**, a term coined by William Whewell in an 1832 review of Charles Lyell's *Principles of Geology* (1830 to 1833), the work that developed Hutton's method and established it across the science.

blocks.text: Modern radiometric dating, the subject of lesson 8, puts the grey beds at Siccar Point at about 435 million years old, laid down on the floor of an ocean that once separated Scotland from England. The overlying red sandstone is about 370 million years old. The unconformity between them therefore spans roughly 65 million years, during which that ocean closed, the grey beds were crumpled in the continental collision, and the resulting mountains were worn down to river plains and fans in a warm, semi-arid climate. Hutton's sense of the scale was sound even without a clock.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Hutton argued that slow, everyday processes could account for the rock record only if the Earth were vastly older than a few thousand years.
Uniformitarianism is the principle of explaining past geological features through processes that can still be observed operating today.
Radiometric dating places the gap at Siccar Point at roughly 65 million years.

blocks.text: Hutton saw the Earth's crust as a self-renewing system. Weather and rivers wear down the land and carry the debris to the sea, where it settles in layers. Buried deep, those layers are compacted and heated into rock, and some are melted outright, before subterranean forces lift them back up as new land to be worn down in turn. The earlier lessons of this course each followed one leg of that loop, which geologists now call the **rock cycle**.

blocks.caption: The rock cycle, with the lessons that covered each step. Rock can also take shortcuts across the loop: igneous rock can weather directly into sediment, and sedimentary rock can be uplifted and eroded without first becoming metamorphic.

blocks.text: Siccar Point catches that loop on its second turn. The grey beds began as loose marine sediment, hardened into rock, were folded and lifted into mountains, and then weathered back into gravel and sand that fed the lower layers of the red sandstone. Since then, the red sandstone has itself been gently tilted and lifted above sea level, and the North Sea waves now batter both formations to make fresh sand on the shore below.

What Hutton could not explain was the engine behind the cycle: what kept the interior of the Earth hot, and what mechanical force could heave a sea floor up into a mountain range. Both answers lay more than a century ahead, and the path toward them began when the most prominent physicist of the nineteenth century calculated how fast the Earth had to be cooling, and concluded that Hutton's abyss of time violated the laws of physics.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The rock cycle connects sediment, sedimentary rock, metamorphic rock, magma and igneous rock through burial, heating, melting, uplift and erosion.
An unconformity shows the cycle turning over: one generation of rock is formed, uplifted and worn down before the next is laid across its remains.

blocks.caption: Five questions on unconformities and deep time
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: At Siccar Point, what evidence in the grey beds themselves shows they were tilted after they formed?
choices: They settled from water as sand and mud, with ripple marks and graded layers that form nearly horizontally
They lie underneath the red sandstone
They contain broken fragments of the red sandstone
items.why: Sediment settling through water forms nearly horizontal layers, and features like ripple marks and graded bedding confirm which way was originally up. Standing at 80 degrees means the beds were rotated after deposition.

items.ask: What do the angular fragments of grey rock inside the lowest layer of the red sandstone prove?
choices: The grey beds were already solid rock and eroding at the surface when the red sand buried them
The grey and red rocks were deposited during the same storm
The red sandstone was injected as a liquid beneath the grey rock
items.why: A layer can only pick up angular rubble of another rock if that other rock is already lithified and exposed to erosion at the surface.

items.ask: What does an unconformity record in a sequence of strata?
choices: A time gap during which rock was eroded away or never deposited at that location
A single catastrophic flood that laid down two rock types at once
A fault plane along which one block of crust slid past another
items.why: An unconformity is a buried erosion surface: millions of years of uplift and wearing down can be represented by a single line between two beds.

items.ask: If deposition and erosion average 0.1 mm per year, roughly how long would it take to lay down and strip away the 11 km of rock involved in the Siccar Point sequence?
items.why: Eleven kilometres is 11,000,000 millimetres; dividing by 0.1 mm per year gives 110 million years.

items.ask: What does the principle of uniformitarianism state?
choices: Past geological features should be explained by the same physical processes that can be observed operating today
Rates of erosion and uplift have remained strictly constant throughout Earth's history
All sedimentary rocks on Earth formed during the same geological period
items.why: Hutton and Lyell argued that observable processes such as river erosion, sedimentation and incremental uplift are sufficient to explain the rock record when given enough time.

summary: **An unconformity is a buried erosion surface.** It separates rocks of very different ages and marks a long gap in the record.
**Siccar Point records a whole cycle.** Marine beds were laid flat, folded upright, raised, worn down, then covered by red sandstone about 65 million years later.
**Slow, everyday processes need vast time.** Hutton reasoned that the Earth must be far older than a few thousand years.
**The present is the key to the past.** Erosion, deposition and uplift we can watch today explain the rocks.
**Rocks are recycled.** Sediment, sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous rock turn into one another through burial, heating, melting, uplift and erosion.
